text.en: Raju tossed a coin and called heads. "What are the chances?" asked his teacher.

An experiment is an action with possible outcomes, like tossing a coin, and the set of all outcomes is the sample space. An event is a part of the sample space. For a finite set of equally likely outcomes, the classical probability is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the total number of outcomes. It lies between zero and one.
The empirical approach finds probability from experiments: P(E) = number of times the event happened / total number of trials. With many comparable independent trials, the observed frequency tends to settle closer to the underlying chance. The fraction can still move closer or farther away in any particular run.
A sure event has probability one and an impossible event has probability zero. An event and its complement are mutually exclusive and together cover all outcomes, so their probabilities add to one.

For a finite set of equally likely outcomes, the classical probability is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the total number of outcomes. It lies between zero and one.
The empirical approach finds probability from experiments: P(E) = number of times the event happened / total number of trials.
With many comparable independent trials, the observed frequency tends to settle closer to the underlying chance. The fraction can still move closer or farther away in any particular run.
A sure event has probability one and an impossible event has probability zero. An event and its complement are mutually exclusive and together cover all outcomes, so their probabilities add to one.
Tossing a coin once is one trial. Head and tail are possible outcomes. Listing both gives the sample space for the ordinary coin model.
Roll a common six-sided die once. Write the six face values, from one to six. A fair die model gives every face the same chance.
The event of rolling an even number consists of outcomes two, four and six. These are three members of the sample space.
An event with one outcome is a simple event. Rolling exactly four is one example. Rolling an even number is a compound event because it includes several outcomes.
In the fair die model, the chance of an even roll is three favourable outcomes over six total outcomes. Reduce the result to one half.
For a sure event, every outcome is favourable. Rolling a number from one to six on the model die is sure. Rolling seven has no favourable outcomes and is impossible.
A spinner with unequal sectors requires another check. There might be three labels, but a label on a wider sector has a better chance. Counting each label once would lose that distinction.
Suppose a blind draw is modelled as equally likely for each counter. A bag contains two red counters and three blue counters. Count the counters as outcomes, even if some share a colour.
For that model, the chance of red is two fifths and the chance of blue is three fifths. The two colours exhaust the possible outcomes in the bag.
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot both happen on the same trial. On one roll, getting a two and getting a five cannot happen together.
Those two events still leave the other four rolls uncovered. Mutually exclusive events are complementary only if they also cover the whole sample space.

board.text: Complementary means no overlap and full coverage

text.en: Rolling at most four and rolling more than four divide the die outcomes into two separate groups that cover all rolls. Either one is the complement of the other.
The chance of more than four is two sixths. To get the chance of at most four, subtract from one. The remaining four sixths agrees with a direct count.
On a single fair die, rolling an even number and rolling a number greater than three can happen together. Four and six lie in both events, so these events overlap.
For two ordinary fair independent coin tosses, list one result at a time in order. Head then tail and tail then head are distinct because they describe different sequences.
Exactly one head means head then tail or tail then head. At least one head also includes two heads. Read the event wording before counting.
For at least one tail, use the complement if that is easier. The only sequence without any tail is head then head. Subtract its one quarter from one.
In an experiment, record how often a selected event occurs. If heads appears fourteen times in twenty tosses, the observed relative frequency is fourteen divided by twenty.
For a model fair coin, the classical probability is one half. In a short trial run the observed fraction can differ. The model and the observed tally answer related questions.
Combine a run of fourteen heads in twenty tosses and a run of ten in twenty. Add the heads together and add the number of tosses together. The pooled observed frequency is twenty-four over forty.
If one run has more trials than another, calculate from their pooled totals. Averaging the two fractions without accounting for different run sizes can give a different result.
If many recorded runs disagree with a fair model, examine how the data were gathered and whether the model makes sense. A small run can also differ just by chance.

text.en: Probabilities of one half can describe very different events, such as a head on a fair coin or an even roll on a fair die. Equal probabilities compare chances across models.
